title: The Tenets of Our Faith · Scripture Challenge

slides.title: THE TENETS OF OUR FAITH
slides.sub: A Scripture challenge · Oneness · Holiness · New Birth
slides.notes: Welcome. Ask before explaining. Do not reveal the answers before the congregation responds.

slides.title: Do you know what you believe, or only what you were taught?
slides.sub: If someone asks you WHY, can you explain it from Scripture?
slides.notes: Poll first, then invite two people to explain their choices.

slides.title: The rules of the challenge
points: One person reads the objection aloud.
Someone offers the strongest opposing interpretation.
Someone offers an Apostolic response.
We read the larger passage, not a detached verse.
We mark: text, interpretation, and unresolved questions.

slides.title: One God is the starting point
slides.text: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:
slides.notes: Connect with Mark 12:29; Isaiah 44:6 and 45:5; do not assert this verse alone disproves the Trinity.

slides.title: CHALLENGE 1 · Who sent whom in Isaiah 48:16?
slides.sub: The speaker says 'the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me.' Doesn't that give us three persons?
slides.notes: Have someone read 48:12–17, not only v16. Ask who 'I' refers to before and after 'and now'.

slides.title: Read the difficult verse
slides.text: Come ye near unto me, hear ye this; I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; from the time that it was, there am I: and now the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me.
slides.notes: Then read 48:12 and 48:17. Punctuation is a presentation issue, not proof that speaker shift occurred.

slides.title: Isaiah 48:16 · Which reading holds?
points: 48:12–13: the speaker is 'the first' and the Creator.
48:16: 'and now' may introduce a prophetic speaker.
48:17: 'Thus saith the LORD' introduces divine speech again.
No original modern quotation marks fix the speaker boundary.
Possible reading ≠ demonstrated fact.
slides.notes: Have the congregation articulate the strongest objection to the prophetic-speaker reading: the shift has no explicit speaker tag.

slides.title: CHALLENGE 2 · Does Genesis 19:24 describe two LORDs?
slides.sub: The LORD rained fire 'from the LORD out of heaven.' Why does Yahweh appear twice?
slides.notes: Ask volunteers to diagram subject, action, source.

slides.title: One LORD, repeated source
slides.text: Then the LORD rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven;

slides.title: CHALLENGE 3 · Who shared glory before the world?
slides.sub: John 17:5 sounds like the Son existed beside the Father before creation.
slides.notes: Invite strongest opposing reading. Do NOT pretend prayer or preexistence language is imaginary.

slides.title: Glory before the world
slides.text: And now, O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with the glory which I had with thee before the world was.

slides.title: CHALLENGE 4 · How can the Word be WITH God?
slides.sub: John 1:1 says the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

slides.title: The Word was God
slides.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

slides.title: CHALLENGE 5 · If Jesus is God, why did He pray?
slides.sub: In Matthew 26:39 Jesus submits His will to the Father's. Is He speaking to Himself?

slides.title: The incarnation is not pretend
points: God is Spirit (John 4:24).
The Word became flesh (John 1:14).
Jesus is fully divine (Colossians 2:9).
Jesus' human obedience and prayer are genuine (Hebrews 5:7–9).
A real relational objection deserves a real explanation.

slides.title: CHALLENGE 6 · Three at the Jordan?
slides.sub: Jesus in the water, the Spirit descending, the Father's voice from heaven.

slides.title: The voice from heaven
slides.text: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.

slides.title: CHALLENGE 7 · Why does the Son become subject?
slides.sub: 1 Corinthians 15 says the Son delivers the kingdom and is subject to God.

slides.title: The Son subject unto God
slides.text: And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all.

slides.title: Can you answer in 30 seconds?
points: Group A: Isaiah 48:16 and punctuation.
Group B: Genesis 19:24 and the repeated LORD.
Group C: John 17:5 and glory.
Group D: John 1:1 and the Word.
Group E: Jesus' baptism and prayer.
Group F: 1 Corinthians 15:24–28.
slides.notes: Allow 5 minutes in groups, 30 seconds per spokesperson, invite fair correction. Optional bonus: Matthew 11:27 with John 1:18 and 2 Corinthians 4:6.

slides.title: HOLINESS · Is holiness mostly about clothing?
slides.sub: 'Holiness is why we do it. Modesty is how we do it.' Is that the whole picture?

slides.title: Be holy in all manner of life
slides.text: But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation;

slides.title: HEAD COVERING · Why does Paul mention angels?
slides.sub: If it were only about other people seeing us, why 'because of the angels'?
slides.notes: No invented details about exactly what angels do. Read 3–16 including 11–12 and 15.

slides.title: Because of the angels
slides.text: For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels.

slides.title: Her hair is given for a covering
slides.text: But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering.

slides.title: BAPTISM · What is the 'name'?
slides.sub: Jesus says 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.' What did the apostles actually say and do?

slides.title: Go, baptizing in the name
slides.text: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:

slides.title: GREEK CHALLENGE · What does ONOMA mean?
slides.sub: Does 'in the name' literally mean 'in the power'? What does the original Greek say?
slides.notes: Invite one guess; distinguish direct meaning from association. Greek phrase is eis to onoma.

slides.title: εἰς τὸ ὄνομα · INTO THE NAME
points: εἰς (eis): into / unto / in
τὸ (to): the (singular article)
ὄνομα (onoma): name (singular)
A name can represent identity, character and authority.
This phrase alone does not specify spoken baptismal words.
slides.notes: A singular name does not by itself prove a singular divine person; this is part of a larger biblical argument.

slides.title: CHALLENGE · Whose name saves?
slides.sub: Matthew commands baptism into 'the name'; Peter says there is no other saving name. How does this inform Acts 2:38?
slides.notes: Read Acts 3:6 and Acts 4:7–12. Peter names Jesus Christ of Nazareth at Acts 4:10.

slides.title: There is none other name
slides.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
slides.notes: Read Acts 4:10–12 in context, not simply a slogan. Peter is discussing healing and salvation through Jesus Christ.

slides.title: What does ONOMA actually mean?
slides.sub: Jesus says all POWER is His, then commands baptism in the NAME. Are those the same Greek word?
slides.notes: Ask first. Launch the Greek poll on the iPad. Let the church distinguish the two words before revealing.

slides.title: ONOMA ≠ EXOUSIA
slides.sub: The name identifies the person; the commission carries His authority.
points: ὄνομα (onoma) = name; can imply identity and represented authority.
εἰς τὸ ὄνομα (eis to onoma) = into the name (v.19).
ἐξουσία (exousia) = authority, rendered “power” in KJV v.18.
The baptismal phrase is not literally “in the power of.”
slides.notes: Do not let the etymology overstate a baptismal conclusion; move from grammar to the Acts narrative.

slides.title: There is none other name
slides.sub: Read Acts 3:6 and 4:7–12 to identify which name Peter means.
slides.text: Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
slides.notes: Ask: whose name had Peter used to heal the lame man? Compare Acts 3:6, 4:10, 4:12.

slides.title: Repent and be baptized
slides.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

slides.title: HOLY GHOST · How do you know you received?
slides.sub: Is it a feeling? A raised hand? Speaking in tongues? The Spirit's ongoing fruit?

slides.title: As the Spirit gave utterance
slides.text: And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.

slides.title: They heard them speak with tongues
slides.text: For they heard them speak with tongues, and magnify God. Then answered Peter,

slides.title: What does the new birth call us to?
points: Repent: turn to God in faith.
Be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.
Receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
Continue in doctrine, fellowship, prayer, and holy living.
slides.notes: Close with response and open questions; don't turn Q&A into pressure toward visitors.

slides.title: CAN YOU GIVE AN ANSWER?
slides.sub: Defend your faith. Test your interpretation. Honor the person asking.
slides.notes: Take anonymous questions. End with prayer.

manuscript.title: THE TENETS OF OUR FAITH
manuscript.html:
Introduction: Tonight, you are going to do some of the work. I am going to give you passages that people use to challenge what we believe. You must read them, explain their context, and make a case. No answer wins because it sounds confident.

Our pattern is Question → Read → Debate → Reveal → Explain → Apply. Faith deserves careful study and a gracious defense (Acts 17:11; 1 Peter 3:15; 2 Timothy 2:24–25).
manuscript.notes: Welcome. Ask before explaining. Do not reveal the answers before the congregation responds.

manuscript.title: Do you know what you believe, or only what you were taught?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: How do you respond when another Christian makes a biblical objection to our doctrine?

Our task is to represent an objection accurately, not to mock it. Classical Trinitarians teach ONE God in three eternally distinct persons, not three gods. We believe the one God is fully manifested in Jesus Christ. The disagreement is about God's personal distinctions, not whether Christians believe in one God.
manuscript.notes: Poll first, then invite two people to explain their choices.

manuscript.title: The rules of the challenge
manuscript.html: We do not claim every passage settles the Trinity debate on its own. Distinction in language is not automatically distinction of eternal persons. But demonstrating an alternative interpretation does not automatically prove Oneness either. Test how well your interpretation accounts for the whole biblical witness.

manuscript.title: One God is the starting point
manuscript.html:
Read Mark 12:29, Isaiah 44:6 and Isaiah 45:5. Both Apostolic Oneness and classical Trinitarian Christians affirm biblical monotheism. What differs is whether Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are eternally distinct persons within that one divine being.

Oneness starting claim: God is one, and Jesus fully reveals the one God (John 1:14; Colossians 2:9). The Son is truly human as well as truly divine. His human prayers and obedience are genuine.
manuscript.notes: Connect with Mark 12:29; Isaiah 44:6 and 45:5; do not assert this verse alone disproves the Trinity.

manuscript.title: CHALLENGE 1 · Who sent whom in Isaiah 48:16?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Who is speaking in Isaiah 48:12–16? Does the speaker stay the same throughout?

A strong Trinitarian reading sees the one who has been present from the beginning sent by the Lord GOD and His Spirit, consistent with preincarnate Christ. The prophetic reading sees an abrupt transition near 'and now,' where Isaiah is sent by the Lord GOD and His Spirit (compare Isaiah 61:1). A genuine challenge: there is no explicit 'then Isaiah said' in the Hebrew. So the prophetic reading is possible but not proved. Original Hebrew manuscripts do not contain modern English quotation marks; punctuation is editorial. The Spirit's grammatical role is disputed too. The text does not explicitly define three coequal, coeternal persons.
manuscript.notes: Have someone read 48:12–17, not only v16. Ask who 'I' refers to before and after 'and now'.

manuscript.title: Read the difficult verse
manuscript.html:
Two readings to put on the screen:

Reading A (continuous speaker): '...from the time that it was, there am I: and now the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me.' This is often read as a divine or messianic speaker distinguished from the LORD who sends and the Spirit.

Reading B (prophetic interjection): '[Divine speech concludes after: there am I.] And now [Isaiah speaks:] the Lord GOD ... hath sent me.' Compare Isaiah 61:1. The bracketed wording is teaching annotation, NOT inspired text and not a claim that quotation marks existed in the Hebrew.

Apostolic response: Sending language by itself does not tell us what ontological distinction exists. Isaiah elsewhere insists on one exclusive LORD. Strongest limitation: this does NOT settle who the speaker is. Mark ambiguity honestly.
manuscript.notes: Then read 48:12 and 48:17. Punctuation is a presentation issue, not proof that speaker shift occurred.

manuscript.title: Isaiah 48:16 · Which reading holds?
manuscript.html: Say: 'The strongest argument against my reading is the unannounced change of speaker. I will acknowledge it. But the strongest argument against calling this a proof of the Trinity is that three eternal divine persons are not stated. It takes more theological interpretation to get there.' Keep the distinction between certainty and plausibility visible.
manuscript.notes: Have the congregation articulate the strongest objection to the prophetic-speaker reading: the shift has no explicit speaker tag.

manuscript.title: CHALLENGE 2 · Does Genesis 19:24 describe two LORDs?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: If a name is repeated as subject and source, must there be two persons?

Trinitarian reading: the LORD on earth invokes judgment from the LORD in heaven. Apostolic response: Hebrew can repeat the same personal name in place of a pronoun or repeat source for emphasis. The most straightforward single-referent reading here is that Yahweh sent judgment from heaven, from Yahweh Himself. But the repetition is real and it can be given a Trinitarian interpretation; the text does not explicitly identify 'Father' and 'Son.'
manuscript.notes: Ask volunteers to diagram subject, action, source.

manuscript.title: One LORD, repeated source
manuscript.html: Read Genesis 18–19. Note who speaks to Abraham, who goes to Sodom, and who sends judgment. The phrase is 'the LORD ... from the LORD out of heaven.' Hebrew repetition of the name is not automatic evidence of two divine persons. Explain it simply: 'The LORD caused fire to rain from heaven as the judgment of the LORD.' This is a defensible reading, not a grammatical certainty that excludes others.

manuscript.title: CHALLENGE 3 · Who shared glory before the world?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Is glory with the Father before the world only a plan, or the Son's personal preexistence?

A strong Trinitarian reading is that the Son personally shared eternal glory with the Father. Our previous Apostolic reading places the incarnate Messiah's promised glory in God's eternal purpose, fulfilled through the resurrection and exaltation (compare John 17:4–5, Acts 2:23, 1 Peter 1:19–20). However, 'I had with thee' naturally sounds relational and is one of the stronger objections. The verse is not disposed of merely by saying 'it was only a plan.' Explain why Scripture sometimes speaks of what is appointed as certain while acknowledging the ordinary force of the words.
manuscript.notes: Invite strongest opposing reading. Do NOT pretend prayer or preexistence language is imaginary.

manuscript.title: Glory before the world
manuscript.html:
John 17:5 is not a throwaway verse. The Apostolic answer: God's Word and redemptive purpose are eternal; the Son enters history through the incarnation. Christ asks for the glory of His completed mission to be realized. Read John 17:4–5 with John 1:1,14 and 1 Peter 1:20.

Important honesty: Some interpreters will find personal preexistence more natural here. A responsible defense must explain the wording and compare all the passages, not announce that opponents have misread a simple text.

manuscript.title: CHALLENGE 4 · How can the Word be WITH God?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Does 'with God' necessarily mean a second divine person?

Our Apostolic account: the Logos is God's own divine Word, self-expression, reason and purpose, eternally belonging to God and fully divine, who becomes flesh in Christ (v14). Trinitarians read this Word as the eternal Son personally distinguished from the Father. John 1:1 makes distinction and deity unavoidable questions, but the nature of that distinction must be argued, not assumed.

manuscript.title: The Word was God
manuscript.html: Read verses 1–3, 14, and 18. For the Oneness view, the Word is never a separate lesser god: it was God Himself, and became flesh. Pair with 2 Corinthians 4:6, Colossians 1:15, and Colossians 2:9. A Trinitarian sees the same text as evidence of both divinity and personal distinction. The challenge is to give a coherent account of both clauses.

manuscript.title: CHALLENGE 5 · If Jesus is God, why did He pray?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Can the one who is fully God truly obey and pray as a man?

Yes, the incarnate Son possesses real humanity, including a human will and human dependence on the Father. Oneness distinguishes God's eternal Spirit and the genuinely human Son without dividing deity into persons. The strongest opposing observation is that the prayers portray personal relationship. Simply saying 'Jesus talked to Himself' fails to honor the text and should never be our answer.

manuscript.title: The incarnation is not pretend
manuscript.html: Do not explain the incarnation as if Jesus were a puppet body. In Gethsemane, Jesus' human will submits to the Father's will. This is real prayer. The Oneness reading maintains that the Father is not a separate deity from the one God present in Christ; Trinitarians maintain a personal distinction between Father and Son. Both are attempting to interpret biblical data.

manuscript.title: CHALLENGE 6 · Three at the Jordan?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Does simultaneous manifestation require three eternal persons?

The Apostolic response: the transcendent God is not confined to Jesus' earthly body; the Spirit's descent and voice from heaven express God's presence and testimony during the baptism of the incarnate Son. A Trinitarian sees coordinated actions of three distinct persons. The event shows the distinctions, but whether those are eternal personal distinctions is a theological conclusion.

manuscript.title: The voice from heaven
manuscript.html: Read Matthew 3:16–17 in full. Never deny the visible sequence. Say: 'God can speak from heaven and act through His Spirit while fully present in Christ.' Oneness theology interprets these as God's manifestations alongside the humanity of the Son. Do not claim Matthew labels them 'modes' or that their coordination alone proves Oneness.

manuscript.title: CHALLENGE 7 · Why does the Son become subject?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: What ends when Christ delivers the kingdom? Does God cease to be God?

Apostolic reading: the Son's mediatorial kingdom reaches completion; the incarnate Messiah has conquered enemies, and God is all in all. This does not mean divine nature is abolished or that Jesus ceases to exist. The passage distinguishes God and the Son in the economy of redemption. Trinitarians interpret the Son's submission in His mediatorial role without denying eternal divine equality. Read the whole argument in verses 20–28.

manuscript.title: The Son subject unto God
manuscript.html: Explain the distinction between the identity of Christ and the mission of Christ as the risen Messiah. 'That God may be all in all' points toward the completion of the mediatorial reign. Compare 1 Timothy 2:5. This is not a proof that Christ stops being God; nor by itself does it disprove Trinitarian distinctions.

manuscript.title: Can you answer in 30 seconds?
manuscript.html: Give groups two minutes to prepare. Each has thirty seconds to state the Trinitarian argument fairly, thirty seconds for the Apostolic response, and one text that might challenge their own interpretation. Bonus: Matthew 11:27 speaks of Father and Son knowing one another exclusively. Compare John 1:18, Colossians 1:15 and 2 Corinthians 4:6 about the invisible God being revealed through Christ. Ask whether revelatory relationship necessarily entails eternal personal distinction.
manuscript.notes: Allow 5 minutes in groups, 30 seconds per spokesperson, invite fair correction. Optional bonus: Matthew 11:27 with John 1:18 and 2 Corinthians 4:6.

manuscript.title: HOLINESS · Is holiness mostly about clothing?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Can someone look modest and still live unholy?

Yes. Holiness is belonging to the holy God; it governs the whole life: motive, compassion, honesty, speech, fidelity, consumption and conduct. Modesty is one outward expression of humility and restraint, not the entirety of holiness (1 Peter 1:15–16; Hebrews 12:14; 1 Timothy 2:9–10). The maxim is memorable, but holiness reaches farther than clothing.

manuscript.title: Be holy in all manner of life
manuscript.html: Read 1 Peter 1:13–16 and Hebrews 12:14. Holiness includes the inner life and outward practice. A heart claim that never alters life is deficient; an outward standard without a yielded heart is also deficient. Ask people to name non-clothing examples of holiness.

manuscript.title: HEAD COVERING · Why does Paul mention angels?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Why is head covering spiritual and not merely a dress rule?

Paul places the practice in the context of prayer, worship, creation and headship. 'Because of the angels' explicitly places angels in his explanation, even though their exact role is not explained. One Apostolic application sees hair or covering as an outward sign of respect for divine order, not a costume for people. The exact question of whether Paul requires cloth covering, long hair, or a first-century custom is debated. Do not state that the angels require a specific hairstyle or that covering earns salvation. Read v10 in light of v5–6, v11–12, and v15.
manuscript.notes: No invented details about exactly what angels do. Read 3–16 including 11–12 and 15.

manuscript.title: Because of the angels
manuscript.html:
Read 1 Corinthians 11:3–16. Compare v10 with v15, which calls long hair a covering. Paul is discussing both the honor of worship and a visible practice. The interpretation within many Apostolic circles emphasizes uncut hair as a spiritual sign of obedience and order. Other Christians interpret an actual fabric covering, or the entire instruction as contextual. Discuss why our conviction reads the passage as it does, then separate that conviction from speculation concerning angels. Verse 10 says 'power' (authority) on her head, and scholars debate precisely what that means.

Say: 'Holiness is not performed for an audience. Our obedience is directed toward God, and Paul asks us to reckon with a spiritual dimension of worship.' Do not claim every modesty practice is explicitly tied to angels.

manuscript.title: Her hair is given for a covering
manuscript.html: Ask: If her hair is a covering, what is the relationship to the covering of verses 5–6? There are more than one serious reading. Teach the church's reasoned practice without disguising inference as quotation. Honor the mutuality Paul affirms in verses 11–12: neither is independent in the Lord.

manuscript.title: BAPTISM · What is the 'name'?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Is Matthew 28:19 contradicted by Acts 2:38?

Apostolic Pentecostals argue that Jesus' singular 'name' is revealed as Jesus Christ and the apostles obeyed His command by baptizing in His name. Read Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5. Other Christians understand Matthew 28:19 as the baptismal words commanded by Jesus and Acts' 'in Jesus' name' as identifying allegiance/authority rather than giving a spoken formula. We need to argue why we follow the apostolic pattern, not pretend the dispute is nonexistent.

manuscript.title: Go, baptizing in the name
manuscript.html: Look closely at the singular 'name' and the three designations. Ask: Which elements are explicit? Matthew mentions Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It does not explicitly spell out 'Jesus' in this verse. The Apostolic reasoning connects Jesus' revealed saving name to the apostolic practice recorded in Acts. Explain the inference plainly.

manuscript.title: GREEK CHALLENGE · What does ONOMA mean?
manuscript.html:
ASK: Is 'name' a literal translation of the Greek, or does onoma literally mean 'power'? Let them answer first.

Matthew uses εἰς τὸ ὄνομα (eis to onoma): roughly 'into the name.' The noun onoma means 'name.' In context, a name can represent someone's identity, reputation, and authority. It does NOT literally translate 'power.' The association with authority is a figure of speech and contextual usage. See Acts 4:7, where the question is explicitly 'by what power, or by what name?'
manuscript.notes: Invite one guess; distinguish direct meaning from association. Greek phrase is eis to onoma.

manuscript.title: εἰς τὸ ὄνομα · INTO THE NAME
manuscript.html:
Walk through the three Greek words. Eis + accusative can mark entry into relationship or belonging. Onoma is singular. An Apostolic reading takes the singular name with apostolic practice in Acts to point to Jesus, the revealed name of salvation. A Trinitarian can accept the singular name while retaining the triadic baptismal wording. Grammar alone does not resolve the disagreement.

Ask why Acts repeatedly speaks of baptism in Jesus Christ's name (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5). Also remind students that Acts' Greek baptismal prepositions vary: the phrases are not word-for-word identical throughout the passages.
manuscript.notes: A singular name does not by itself prove a singular divine person; this is part of a larger biblical argument.

manuscript.title: CHALLENGE · Whose name saves?
manuscript.html:
ASK: Which saving name is Peter speaking about? Read Acts 4:10: Jesus Christ of Nazareth. Then read verse 12.

Apostolic reasoning: Jesus commissions baptism into 'the name'; Peter preaches Jesus as the saving name and calls people to baptism in Jesus Christ's name (Acts 2:38). Together these give the church its reason for administering baptism in Jesus' name.

Counterargument: Acts 4:12 teaches exclusive salvation through Christ, but does not directly prescribe the spoken words during baptism. Other Christians hold the Matthew 28:19 language is the proper wording. Do not overclaim what one verse proves.
manuscript.notes: Read Acts 3:6 and Acts 4:7–12. Peter names Jesus Christ of Nazareth at Acts 4:10.

manuscript.title: There is none other name
manuscript.html:
Read Acts 4:7: 'By what power, or by what name, have ye done this?' Read verse 10: Peter answers that it was by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. Then read 4:12. The 'name' refers to Jesus and His saving authority, not a magical syllable.

Teacher summary: 'The power belongs to the person. The name identifies Him and invokes His authority. That is why the Apostolic response in Acts 2:38 matters.'
manuscript.notes: Read Acts 4:10–12 in context, not simply a slogan. Peter is discussing healing and salvation through Jesus Christ.

manuscript.title: What does ONOMA actually mean?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: Does the Greek word translated “name” in Matthew 28:19 literally mean “power”? If not, what does it mean, and why does the context make authority important?

Have someone read verses 18 AND 19. In verse 18 Jesus declares that all exousia (authority) has been given to Him. Verse 19 then commands baptism eis to onoma, “into the name.” Do not treat onoma as the literal Greek for power. It is the word for name, and in context a name can refer to the person, authority, and allegiance represented by that name.
manuscript.notes: Ask first. Launch the Greek poll on the iPad. Let the church distinguish the two words before revealing.

manuscript.title: ONOMA ≠ EXOUSIA
manuscript.html:
Word study: ὄνομα (onoma, pronounced ON-oh-mah) is the ordinary Greek noun for “name.” It can stand for a person's identity, standing, or authority. In Matthew 28:19 the full phrase is εἰς τὸ ὄνομα (eis to onoma), literally “into the name.” It can convey being identified with or entering allegiance to the named one. This interpretation is about how the phrase is used; it does not turn onoma into a different word.

Contrast: Matthew 28:18: πᾶσα ἐξουσία (pasa exousia) = “all authority.” KJV renders that “All power.” Exousia means authority or the right to act. The word dynamis also means power in other NT passages, but it is not the noun Jesus uses in Matthew 28:18 or 28:19.

Apostolic argument: The risen Jesus has all authority (v.18), gives the command to baptize into the singular “name” (v.19), and the apostles repeatedly baptize in the name of Jesus Christ or the Lord Jesus (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5). Our conviction is that Peter and the apostles carried out the command rather than contradicting it.

Fair counter-reading: Trinitarians also recognize the singular Greek noun onoma, but read “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit” as the wording of Jesus' baptismal command, with Acts emphasizing the authority or allegiance represented by Jesus' name. The Greek word alone does not resolve that theological dispute.
manuscript.notes: Do not let the etymology overstate a baptismal conclusion; move from grammar to the Acts narrative.

manuscript.title: There is none other name
manuscript.html:
READ IN CONTEXT: After the healing at the temple, the authorities ask in Acts 4:7, “By what power, or by what name, have ye done this?” In verse 10 Peter explicitly names Jesus Christ of Nazareth, and in verse 12 declares that salvation is in no other.

ASK: If this is the name through which salvation comes, why is the name of Jesus so central to Apostolic preaching and baptism?

Explain: Acts 4:12 is about the exclusivity of salvation in Jesus, not a stand-alone transcript of a baptismal ceremony. Link it to the recorded practice: Acts 2:38, 8:16, 10:48 and 19:5. Do not build the whole formula argument on one lexical definition.

30-second answer for the congregation: Jesus possesses all authority. Jesus commanded baptism in the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The apostles baptized in Jesus' name. Acts 4:12 identifies Jesus as the only saving name. We understand the apostolic practice as obedience to Jesus' command.
manuscript.notes: Ask: whose name had Peter used to heal the lame man? Compare Acts 3:6, 4:10, 4:12.

manuscript.title: Repent and be baptized
manuscript.html: Read Acts 2:37–39 aloud. Peter calls for repentance, baptism in Jesus Christ's name for forgiveness, and promises the gift of the Holy Ghost. Compare Acts 8:16; 10:48; 19:5 and Acts 4:12. Baptism does not mechanically save through syllables; the response is to the risen Jesus in repentance and faith. Apostolic practice uses His name explicitly.

manuscript.title: HOLY GHOST · How do you know you received?
manuscript.html:
ASK THE ROOM: What is the biblical evidence when someone initially receives the Holy Ghost?

Classical Apostolic Pentecostal teaching regards Spirit-given speaking in other tongues as the initial outward evidence, citing Acts 2:4, 10:44–46, and 19:6. Acts 8 describes an observable result without directly naming tongues; not every reception account gives the same details. Other Christian traditions disagree that tongues is universally required. Tongues are not produced by coaching or imitation. Fruit and a transformed life are important evidence of ongoing work of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23); never confuse initial sign with total spiritual maturity.

manuscript.title: As the Spirit gave utterance
manuscript.html: Acts 2:4: the believers spoke in other tongues as the Spirit gave utterance. Acts 10:46: Gentile believers were heard speaking in tongues and magnifying God. Acts 19:6: disciples spoke in tongues and prophesied. Explain why Apostolic believers take this pattern seriously while admitting that narrative pattern and universal doctrinal requirement are not identical claims.

manuscript.title: They heard them speak with tongues
manuscript.html: Read Acts 10:44–48. The Jewish witnesses recognized the outpouring because they heard them speak with tongues and exalt God. This is a strong Pentecostal text because the narrative identifies an observable sign in the moment. Do not demand emotional theatrics. The Spirit gives utterance, not a human instructor.

manuscript.title: What does the new birth call us to?
manuscript.html: Read John 3:5 and Acts 2:38–42. This is not only an argument over formulas. We are responding to Christ's gospel. Invite sincere questions. If someone wants baptism, prayer, or further Bible study, connect them with leadership. Close by reminding the church: conviction, humility, worship, and real life must align.
manuscript.notes: Close with response and open questions; don't turn Q&A into pressure toward visitors.

manuscript.title: CAN YOU GIVE AN ANSWER?
manuscript.html:
Closing challenge: Be able to say, 'This is what the text says. This is how we understand it. Here is why. Here is the strongest question someone might still ask.' A conviction that survives an honest question becomes more than repetition.

Prayer: God, give us conviction that is rooted in Scripture, holiness that reaches the heart, and courage to obey the gospel with humility and love. Amen.
manuscript.notes: Take anonymous questions. End with prayer.
